cards.definition: Seven open-ended machine-learning research-engineering environments built from scratch so models have not been trained on them — e.g. fitting a scaling law, writing a GPU kernel that minimizes prefix-sum runtime, designing a model architecture under unusual constraints. Each environment gives the agent (human or AI) a computer with GPUs, a scoring function, and a fixed time limit; the instruction is to score as high as possible. Scores are calibrated so 0 equals the starting solution and 1 equals METR's reference solution.

The benchmark was calibrated against 71 paid eight-hour attempts by 61 distinct human experts, all attempting the same environments with the same resources and information as the AI agents. Per the paper: 82% of expert attempts reached a non-zero score and 24% matched or exceeded METR's strong reference solutions. This head-to-head design is what makes RE-Bench's human-vs-agent comparisons faithful rather than apples-to-oranges.

At a 2-hour total budget per environment, the best AI agents scored 4x higher than human experts. But humans have better returns to time: at 8 hours humans narrowly exceeded top agent scores, and at 32 total hours (across attempts) humans reached 2x the top agent score. The qualitative finding: agents generate and test implementations more than ten times faster than humans at much lower cost, yet often fail to react appropriately to novel information or build on earlier progress within a single run.

On a prefix-sum GPU-kernel task, OpenAI's o1-preview wrote a custom CUDA kernel achieving 0.64 ms — beating the best human expert's 0.67 ms (starting code ran at 4.74 ms; METR's reference solution at 1.60 ms). The example shows agents' strength in rapid, high-volume experimentation: they can discover genuinely novel implementations humans missed within the same environment.

RE-Bench exists because frontier AI safety policies treat automation of AI R&D by AI agents as a capability of concern — METR cites the White House National Security Memorandum on AI and the EU AI Act. The benchmark is a measuring instrument for the recursive-self-improvement question: whether AI systems can do the research engineering that would let them improve themselves. It does not claim to settle that question.

METR states the time horizon as the human-expert task length at which an agent has an x% chance of success, commonly the 50% (P50) or 80% (P80) success level. The procedure: time human experts on a diverse suite of multi-step software and research tasks, fit a logistic curve of model success against human task length, and read the task length where the curve crosses the chosen probability. At the March 2025 measurement, models succeeded near 100% on sub-4-minute human tasks and under 10% on tasks over ~4 hours.

The 50%-reliability task horizon of frontier models has doubled roughly every 7 months from 2019 through the 2025 measurement (P50 doubling time ~196 days, 95% confidence interval [162, 223]). METR's sensitivity analysis: even a 10x error in absolute measurement would shift the forecast date for month-long tasks by only ~2 years, because the trend is steep and smooth on a log scale. A separate replication on SWE-bench Verified found an even faster doubling, under 3 months.

In January 2026 METR refreshed its estimates as Time Horizon 1.1: the suite grew from 170 to 228 tasks (+34%), long tasks (8h+ human time) doubled from 14 to 31, and evaluation infrastructure moved from METR's in-house Vivaria to the UK AI Security Institute's open-source Inspect framework. The long-run doubling stays ~7 months, but the post-2023 trend is 20% faster: P50 doubling of 130.8 days (CI [107, 161]) vs 165.3 days under TH1. METR notes the speedup is partly a genuinely faster recent trajectory and partly a suite-composition change; new estimates fall within TH1 confidence intervals.

The time horizon is a fitted, suite-specific estimate of autonomous task-completion capability. It is not a claim that models can automate whole jobs or research organizations, nor that a model 'works for 16 hours' in any ordinary sense. METR itself flags that measurements above ~16 hours are unreliable with the current suite, and that the trend is sensitive to task composition — 26 of TH1.1's 31 long tasks use estimated rather than measured human times.
cards.term: What the metric does not claim

cards.definition: RE-Bench's authors list real limitations: only 7 environments are released (most are held back to stay uncontaminated); the tasks have clearer objectives and faster feedback loops than real ML research, where goals are ambiguous and feedback can take months; and the difficulty ceiling is finite — saturating the benchmark would mean agents significantly outperforming top ML engineers in this setting. For time horizons: the trend is an extrapolation of a specific fitted quantity, and robustness checks do not remove model error about external validity.

1) What exactly is the benchmark's comparison set — are humans and agents truly given the same environments, resources, and time? 2) How were the tasks selected and vetted (contamination, solvability, scoring integrity)? 3) Are human baselines measured or estimated? 4) What changes when the suite or infrastructure changes (TH1→TH1.1 moved the post-2023 doubling estimate by 20%)? 5) What would it take to falsify the headline trend? A benchmark's value lives in these answers, not in its headline numbers.

objectives: Describe RE-Bench's design: 7 contamination-free environments, calibrated scoring, faithful human baselines
Explain the crossover finding: agents win at 2-hour budgets, humans at 8-hour and 32-hour budgets, and why
State the motivation behind RE-Bench: measuring AI automation of AI R&D as a capability of concern
Define the time-horizon metric and how it is fitted from human task times and model success curves
Report the ~7-month doubling trend (2019-2025) and the TH1.1 update's faster post-2023 estimate (130.8 days)
Identify the limits of both instruments: RE-Bench's seven environments and fast feedback loops; time horizons as suite-specific fitted estimates
Apply a critical checklist to any capability evaluation: comparison fairness, contamination, baselining quality, and suite-sensitivity
